blood flow and vascular resistance to the legs during maximal exercise are lower in healthy older than in young subjects.
1. During peak exercise, leg blood flow is lower in older compared to younger subjects, due to reduced cardiac output and leg vascular conductance;
leg vascular conductance is reduced with advancing age during peak exercise and that the age-related differences in leg vascular conductance are due to central and peripheral limitations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of blood flow to exercising skeletal muscle during aging.
the effects of physiological and pathophysiological aging on the regulation of skeletal muscle blood flow and its functional consequences.
defining the effects of aging on the control of blood flow to active muscle during exercise, and with identifying the mechanisms underlying these changes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of aging on leg blood flow and its regulation during submaximal and maximal exercise are complex, gender-specific, and training status-dependent.

older subjects have lower leg blood flow during peak exercise and, depending on the intensity of the submaximal exercise and the gender and physical activity status of the subject, may have similar, lower, or higher leg blood flow than young subjects.
older men and women are less able than young subjects to increase leg blood flow during exercise.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the aging process results in reduced leg blood flow during exercise in healthy, non-endurance-trained older subjects, and that the mechanisms underlying this reduction are multifactorial.

aging is associated with a reduction in the capacity of the heart and peripheral circulation to deliver blood to active skeletal muscle during exercise, which may be related in part to altered local mechanisms regulating vascular tone.

older persons are able to achieve a given level of muscle blood flow at higher muscle perfusion pressures than younger subjects, and this is due to a combination of central and peripheral limitations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
leg vascular responses to exercise are altered by aging and gender, but that these changes vary depending on the exercise protocol and the physiological characteristics of the study subjects.
older persons can exercise to their hearts' content, but they may need more blood flow to do so.
the age-related decline in leg blood flow and functional capacity is not inevitable, but rather can be attenuated or reversed by regular physical training.
